chief_complaint: recurrent unexplained polymicrobial sepsis episodes with discovery of syringes containing fecal matter inside hospital room belongings
hpi_details: She is a 35-year-old healthcare worker with 15 admissions for fever of unknown origin. Staff have documented IV-line tampering and contaminated fluid exposure. Treat suspected sepsis urgently while the multidisciplinary team reviews records and addresses immediate safety; the history raises concern for factitious disorder imposed on self, not a diagnosis to confront solely on this encounter.
ideas: She does not identify a psychiatric explanation for the recurrent infections.
concerns: She is concerned about the current infection and hospital treatment.
expectations: She hopes to be admitted to the hospital and started on potent intravenous antibiotics until her fevers completely disappear.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Factitious disorder imposed on self: evaluation and management
core_concepts: Factitious disorder imposed on self involves falsification or induction of illness in the absence of obvious external incentives; diagnosis requires careful, corroborated evidence.
Acute infection and other genuine illness must be assessed and treated on their merits.
Use a coordinated multidisciplinary approach, objective documentation, and one treatment team to reduce iatrogenic harm and inconsistent responses.
Assess suicide and self-harm risk, capacity, trauma history, comorbid mental illness, and risk to others; follow safeguarding and institutional policies where relevant.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent unexplained polymicrobial sepsis episodes with discovery of syringes containing fecal matter inside hospital room belongings

Key HPI features: 35F healthcare worker with 15 prior hospitalizations for fever of unknown origin found tampering with IV lines and injecting contaminated tap water into catheters to assume patient role without external financial incentives requiring psychiatric intervention.
Objective/Exam findings: Assess and treat possible sepsis urgently; preserve objective documentation, review records, and involve infection control and the treating medical team.
common_misconceptions: Assuming recurrent or unusual infection is fabricated before completing appropriate medical assessment.
Equating factitious disorder with malingering; external incentives distinguish them.
Using pejorative language or an adversarial confrontation.
dangerous_errors: Delaying sepsis treatment or failing to protect IV access while investigating the behaviour.
Making an unsupported accusation or sharing allegations beyond the need-to-know clinical and safeguarding team.
Missing acute self-harm, suicide risk, impaired capacity, or risk to vulnerable others.
management_principles: Treat acute infection and use proportionate observation and line-access safeguards under local policy.
Coordinate medical, psychiatric, nursing, infection-control, risk-management, and safeguarding input with clear documentation.
Offer a nonjudgmental psychiatric assessment and longitudinal therapeutic engagement; treat comorbid disorders when present.
Escalate immediately for sepsis, suicidal intent, serious self-injury, incapacity, or risk to another person.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: She has recurrent febrile admissions and reports concern about the current illness. The record documents IV-line tampering and contaminated syringes among her belongings.
reference_soap.objective: Assess for and urgently manage sepsis. Obtain objective records across admissions, document observed events, assess mental state, capacity, suicide/self-harm risk, and risk to others, and involve infection control and the multidisciplinary team.
reference_soap.assessment: The documented behaviour raises concern for factitious disorder imposed on self, while genuine infection must be treated and malingering or other explanations considered.
reference_soap.plan: Protect line access and reduce iatrogenic harm within local policy, coordinate one clinical team, and arrange psychiatric consultation using a non-punitive approach. Urgently escalate for sepsis, suicidal intent, severe self-injury, incapacity, or safeguarding concerns.

differentials: Munchausen syndrome by proxy (if others involved)

must_ask.say: Can you walk me through when these infections have occurred and what treatments have helped?
Given your healthcare background, have you had access to needles or IV supplies outside of work?
Have you had prior psychiatric evaluations, or a history of unexplained medical problems?
What does being in the hospital and being cared for mean to you?
Would you be willing to have your medical records reviewed across hospitals?

history.answer: My fever spiked again this morning with intense shaking chills, and I feel terribly sick like the previous times.
The fever began suddenly yesterday evening around 8 PM and has stayed high since then.
My temperature reached 38.8 degrees Celsius at home, and I had violent shaking chills followed by sweating.
I took 1000 mg of acetaminophen six hours ago, but it only dropped my temperature slightly for an hour before it climbed back up.
No, I do not have any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or shortness of breath.
No burning, no increased frequency, and no pain in my lower back or sides when I urinate.
No, I haven't had any stomach cramps, diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting.
I have a mild throbbing headache from the high fever, but my neck feels completely loose and my thinking is clear.
No, I haven't noticed any skin eruptions, black scabs, insect bites, or joint swelling.
I wake up drenched in sweat when the fever breaks, but my weight has been completely stable over the past six months.
No, I haven't noticed any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No, I haven't traveled abroad, gone hiking in tall grass, or handled farm animals or pets.
No one at my home or workplace has had a fever or similar symptoms.
No, I have never had cancer, chemotherapy, or taken oral steroids or immunosuppressive drugs.
I have never had heart murmurs, rheumatic fever, or valve surgery, and I haven't had any dental procedures recently.
No, I haven't started any new prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, or herbal supplements recently.
I am currently in a monogamous relationship, and I have never used illicit recreational drugs or non-prescribed needles.
This is my fifteenth hospital admission over the past two years for high fevers and blood infections that doctors could never pinpoint.
I work as a hospital nurse, so I handle IV tubing, needles, and flushes every shift, but I strictly follow sterile technique.
I have never seen a psychiatrist or therapist, and I don't feel depressed; this is entirely a physical bacterial infection.
Being in the hospital is exhausting and scary, but at least here the doctors take my infections seriously and keep me safe.
You can look through all my past records and lab reports if it helps figure out why I keep getting these infections.
I was diagnosed with essential hypertension and mild high cholesterol four years ago.
I have been hospitalized fifteen times for recurrent fevers and sepsis, but I have never had any surgeries.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, latex, or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month, and nothing in the past two weeks.
I work as a staff nurse on an inpatient medical ward and live alone in an apartment.
My mother has high blood pressure and my father had a heart attack at sixty, but nobody in the family has recurrent fevers or immune disorders.
My last menstrual period started exactly two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, and there is no chance I am pregnant.
I'm hoping you'll start me on stronger IV antibiotics immediately and keep me admitted until my blood cultures come back completely clear.

exam.finding: Ill-appearing, flushed, and diaphoretic, lying in bed but alert and oriented.
Blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, body temperature 38.7°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Posterior pharynx is clear without erythema or tonsillar exudates; oral mucosa is moist.
Tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray bilaterally with normal light reflexes.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpated.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, rales, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Soft and non-distended without tenderness, guarding, rebound tenderness, or organomegaly.
No rash, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, or eschar; peripheral IV site in right forearm shows mild erythema without purulence.
Supple neck with full active and passive flexion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Alert, cooperative, and attentive; speech is coherent and linear; no overt psychotic features or acute distress.
